statement: In how many ways can 8 identical sweets be shared between 3 children so that each child gets at least one?

choices.misconception: I treated shares that differ only by which child gets what as the same.
I counted only the shares where all three children get different amounts.
I gave each child one sweet, then put the two dividers in different gaps between the 5 sweets left, so no child could get none of the rest.
I allowed a child to receive nothing, which the question forbids.

hints: Give each child one sweet first, then share the rest freely.
Hand out one sweet to each child to satisfy the condition, then the remaining sweets can be split any way at all. Counting those free splits is a standard gaps-between-items count.
After one each, 5 sweets remain to split between 3 children with no restriction.

solutions.reliable: Give each child one sweet, leaving 5 to split freely between 3 children. Lining up the 5 sweets and 2 dividers makes 7 positions, and choosing which 2 are dividers gives 7 x 6 / 2 = 21. The transferable idea: satisfy a minimum first, then count the unrestricted remainder, which turns a constrained problem into a standard one.
solutions.elegant: Five sweets and two dividers in a row is seven positions, and choosing which two are dividers gives the count.

whyOnTest: Clearing the minimum before counting is the move that makes these tractable, and the unrestricted count is on offer.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
